lab_title: Human Heart Anatomy and Blood Flow
top_level_objectives: Identify the four chambers of the heart and the major vessels connected to them.
Trace the route of blood through the heart and explain the pulmonary and systemic circuits.
Explain how the heart valves prevent backflow and support one-way blood flow.
Compare the left and right ventricles and relate wall thickness to pumping demand.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the heart’s overall shape and orient students to the front, back, top, and bottom so later structures can be placed in context.
key_visuals: A realistic external heart model centered in view with the apex pointing down and left.
Highlighted great vessels at the top of the heart.
Subtle labels for the right and left sides from the viewer’s perspective.
student_actions: Rotate the heart to identify anterior, posterior, superior, and inferior surfaces.
Locate the apex and base of the heart.
Notice which side is anatomically right versus left.

scenes.brief_purpose: Help students identify the four chambers and understand their basic roles as receiving or pumping chambers.
key_visuals: A cutaway view revealing all four chambers.
Clear visual separation between atria and ventricles.
Labels for right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, and left ventricle.
student_actions: Tap each chamber to name it and observe its position.
Compare the thinner upper atria with the larger lower ventricles.
State which chambers receive blood and which chambers pump blood out.

scenes.scene_name: Major Vessels and Valve Entry Points
scenes.brief_purpose: Connect the chambers to the major vessels entering and leaving the heart and introduce the valves as directional gates.
key_visuals: Superior and inferior vena cava entering the right atrium.
Pulmonary arteries leaving the right ventricle and pulmonary veins entering the left atrium.
Visible tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral/bicuspid, and aortic valves at the chamber exits.
student_actions: Match each major vessel to the chamber it connects with.
Identify each valve as the structure between a chamber and its outflow tract.
Observe how the valves align with the direction of blood flow.

scenes.brief_purpose: Trace deoxygenated blood from the body through the right side of the heart to the lungs, emphasizing the sequence of structures and one-way flow.
key_visuals: An animated flow path from the vena cavae to the right atrium, right ventricle, and pulmonary arteries.
Directional arrows showing movement toward the lungs.
student_actions: Follow the blood path step by step through the right heart.
Name the tricuspid and pulmonary valves at the correct points in the route.
Explain where blood is oxygenated after leaving the heart.

scenes.scene_name: Systemic Circuit Trace and Left Ventricle Wall Thickness
scenes.brief_purpose: Trace oxygenated blood from the lungs through the left side of the heart to the body and relate the thicker left ventricle wall to the demands of systemic circulation.
key_visuals: An animated flow path from pulmonary veins to left atrium, left ventricle, and aorta.
A visibly thicker left ventricular wall compared with the right ventricle.
Directional arrows showing blood being distributed to the body.
student_actions: Follow the oxygenated blood route through the mitral valve and aortic valve.
Compare the left and right ventricles in size and wall thickness.
Explain why the left ventricle must generate greater pressure.

scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate understanding of valve function by showing how they prevent reverse flow during contraction and relaxation.
key_visuals: A simplified cardiac cycle with valves opening and closing at the appropriate times.
Brief visual moments of backflow being blocked by closed valves.
All four valves highlighted in sequence.
student_actions: Observe when each valve opens or closes during the cycle.
Predict what would happen if a valve failed to close properly.
Summarize how valves ensure one-way blood movement through the heart.
